title: Beirut Emerges as Arab World's Financial and Commercial Hub
reason: Multiple independent sources corroborate that Beirut developed into the Arab world's financial and commercial hub beginning in the early-to-mid 1950s, driven by Lebanon's liberal, unregulated free-market economy and banking sector, which attracted Arab capital fleeing nationalization/instability in Syria, Egypt, and Iraq, plus petrodollar flows from the Gulf. Contributing factors dated to this period: the 1950 breakdown of the Lebanon-Syria customs union (giving Lebanon independent liberal economic policy), Beirut picking up Haifa's role as regional commercial center after the 1948 war, the founding of Intra Bank in 1951, rapid growth in bank numbers (9 in 1945 to 85 by 1960), and the formal 1956 banking secrecy law that cemented the model. Sources describe Beirut/Lebanon as 'the Switzerland of the Middle East' and the region's banking/services capital through the 1950s-1960s. The event description itself frames this as a gradual process 'during the early 1950s' rather than a single-day event, and the substance (liberal banking laws, free-market economy, capital inflows, services economy, East-West bridge role) matches historical accounts closely. Country (Lebanon) and general timeframe (early 1950s) are both confirmed by independent sources.

title: Lebanese Republic Consolidates Post-Independence Institutions
reason: All material facts check out against independent sources: Bechara El Khoury was President of Lebanon from 21 Sept 1943 to 18 Sept 1952 (confirmed by Lebanon's official presidency.gov.lb page and Wikipedia), so he was indeed president in 1950. The National Pact of 1943 — an unwritten power-sharing agreement between President El Khoury and PM Riad Al Solh dividing top offices among Maronite Christians (presidency), Sunni Muslims (premiership), and Shia Muslims (speakership) — is well documented as the foundational governance arrangement that remained in force through this period (Wikipedia's National Pact article, moulahazat.com's founding-fathers piece, presidency.gov.lb). Sources on Lebanon's bureaucracy (countrystudies.us/Library of Congress-derived) confirm the modern civil service and administrative structure trace to this 1943 pact and that post-independence institution-building continued through the early 1950s, consistent with the description of establishing "a functioning bureaucracy and diplomatic presence." The description is a general/vague characterization of an ongoing consolidation process rather than a single discrete incident, but every specific claim in it (country, year, president's identity and tenure, National Pact terms and date) is independently corroborated and none is contradicted.

title: Beirut National Museum Reopens After Civil War Damage
reason: Multiple independent sources (Wikipedia, the National Heritage Foundation's own project page at lebanonheritage.org, The National newspaper, and travel/heritage sites) confirm: the museum closed in 1975 at the civil war's outbreak; it sat on the Green Line front between warring factions and suffered severe shelling/bullet damage and looting; staff (director Maurice Chehab) encased large artifacts like mosaics and sarcophagi in protective concrete and sandbags while smaller items were hidden in a walled-up basement; the building is in a French-inspired Egyptian Revival style; a restoration campaign ran 1995/96-1999 led by the Ministry of Culture, Directorate General of Antiquities, and National Heritage Foundation (architect Jean-Michel Wilmotte), with Wikipedia explicitly stating "UNESCO, the Italian government, and various private foundations provided crucial financial aid, technical expertise, and training"; and the ground and first floors reopened to the public in October 1999 (basement stayed closed until 2016). One minor wrinkle: sources split on the exact day — Wikipedia/lebanonheritage.org cite October 8, 1999 (official ceremony under President Lahoud) while other sources (e.g., encounterstravel.com) cite October 13, 1999 for reopening to the public, plausibly reflecting a ceremonial-vs-public-opening distinction within the same month. Given every other substantive detail is independently corroborated, this is assessed as materially TRUE.

title: Lebanon's Banking System Collapses; Country Defaults for the First Time
reason: Core event fully corroborated by multiple independent authoritative sources: Lebanon's liquidity crisis became visible in August 2019 (black-market rate diverging from the 1997-set 1,507.5 LBP/USD peg) and deepened after the October 17, 2019 protests, with banks unilaterally imposing ad hoc capital controls and restricting dollar withdrawals despite no formal capital-control law (confirmed via Wikipedia 'Lebanese liquidity crisis' page, citing period sources). On March 7, 2020, PM Hassan Diab announced Lebanon would not repay the $1.2bn Eurobond due March 9, triggering the country's first-ever sovereign default — this exact detail (PM name, amount, 'first in history') is corroborated by RT, Al Arabiya, and Executive Magazine. Poverty: ESCWA/UN reporting shows poverty reached 74% (income) to 82% (multidimensional) of the population by September 2021, so 'more than two-thirds' is directionally correct (actually an understatement). Currency: multiple sources (PBS, World Bank coverage, 961) describe the pound as having lost 'about/more than 98%' of its value versus the peg — a figure widely used to describe the overall crisis, though most precisely dated to 2022-2023 rather than strictly 'early 2022' (January 2022 black-market rate of ~27,600-30,000 LBP/USD implies closer to ~93-95% loss at that specific point). GDP: the description's '$55B to $35B' figure roughly matches the widely-cited World Bank estimate for 2020 (GDP fell from ~$55B in 2018 to ~$33B in 2020), but by 'early 2022' — the point the sentence attaches it to — nominal GDP had actually fallen much further, to roughly $21-23 billion (Trading Economics/World Bank data: 2021 ≈ $23.1B, 2022 ≈ $21.0B). So the GDP figure is materially understated/mistimed for the stated period (overstates 2022 GDP by roughly 40-60%), even though it is an accurate figure for an earlier point (2020) in the same crisis. Because the headline event (banking collapse, capital controls, peg break, first-ever sovereign default in March 2020) is precisely confirmed for country=Lebanon, year=2019 (onset), but one quantitative supporting detail (GDP level attributed to 'early 2022') is off by a material margin relative to the actual contemporaneous figure, this is a PARTIAL rather than a clean TRUE.
